title: Manor of St. George
summary: Established in 1696 by Colonel William Tangier Smith, the Manor of St. George sits on Unkechaug homelands and is deeply tied to the early colonial economy of Long Island. Smith documented labor transactions with Unkechaug Native whalers and workers in The Pigskin Book (1696–1721), a record that reveals how Indigenous labor and maritime knowledge sustained coastal industries during a period of near-shore whaling carried out in small cedar boats. After Smith’s death, the ledger continued with indenture agreements.

why_this_matters: The detailed labor transactions recorded in the Manor's "Pigskin Book" between 1696 and 1721 reveal that Unkechaug whalers and workers were the primary economic engine of this vast colonial estate. Acknowledging these records shifts the historical focus from wealthy European landowners to the essential, yet often overlooked, Indigenous maritime knowledge that actually built Long Island's early commercial economy.
introduction_content: The manor was also home to Reverend Peter John Cuffee, an Unkechaug preacher born in Hay Ground in 1712, who later ministered across Long Island, including to the Shinnecock Nation. His grandson and successor, Reverend Paul Cuffee, a Shinnecock man, continued this work before being buried on the Poosepatuck Reservation. In January 2026, the site became a place of Indigenous return when the Unkechaug Nation held a winter solstice and whale ceremony at the Manor—reasserting spiritual presence, continuity, and responsibility to ancestors on land long shaped by colonial control.
land_loss_content: In May of 1691, a tract of land eastward from Connecticut (Carman's) River to the Mastic (Forge) River was purchased from Unkechaug Indian, John Mayhew. A patent for this land was granted by New York Gov. Fletcher on Oct. 9, 1693. This included the beachfront from Huntington East Gut (Old Inlet) to "Cuptwauge" (Cupsogue) at the Southampton Town line. This included the islands near the beach. This property ran north to what today is Middle Country Road. These lands were confirmed under the title of St. George's Manor.
